title: Curve Sketching
body:
Reading the shape of a graph off $f'$ and $f''$ without plotting points. The premise is that two
derivatives carry all the qualitative information: the first says which way the curve is going, the
second says which way it is bending.

| Quantity | Sign | Meaning |
|---|:-:|---|
| $f'$ | $+$ | increasing |
| $f'$ | $-$ | decreasing |
| $f''$ | $+$ | **concave up**, holds water, slopes increasing |
| $f''$ | $-$ | **concave down**, spills, slopes decreasing |

## Critical points

A **critical point** is where $f'(x) = 0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. Extrema can only happen at
critical points (or endpoints), which is what makes the search finite.

> **Not every critical point is an extremum.** $f(x) = x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$ and no max or min
> there, just a flat spot on the way up. This is why there is a test rather than a rule.

**First derivative test**: look at the sign of $f'$ on each side of the critical point.

```
 f' :  + → −     local maximum
 f' :  − → +     local minimum
 f' :  + → +     neither (flat spot)
 f' :  − → −     neither
```

**Second derivative test**: at a critical point $c$,

- $f''(c) > 0$: concave up, so it is a local **minimum**
- $f''(c) < 0$: concave down, so it is a local **maximum**
- $f''(c) = 0$: **inconclusive**, fall back to the first derivative test

The second test is faster when $f''$ is easy; the first is the one that always works.

## Inflection points

Where **concavity changes**, that is, where $f''$ changes sign. $f'' = 0$ alone is not enough:
$f(x) = x^4$ has $f''(0) = 0$ and is concave up on both sides, so there is no inflection there. Same
logical shape as the critical-point warning above, one derivative higher.

## The full procedure

1. Domain, and any symmetry
2. Intercepts
3. Asymptotes: vertical where the denominator vanishes, horizontal from $\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}$
   ([[Limit]])
4. $f'$: critical points, intervals of increase and decrease, classify the extrema
5. $f''$: concavity intervals, inflection points
6. Draw the only curve consistent with all of it

Steps 3 to 5 are a sign chart each. In practice the sketch is a byproduct: what the course is
really teaching is that the sign of a derivative is a claim about behaviour on a whole interval,
which is exactly what the [[Mean Value Theorem]] licenses.
